dailyBrief.text: Overnight, the war and the diplomacy collided: Russia and Ukraine traded huge overnight strikes just hours after Moscow agreed in principle to resume peace talks, with Kyiv hit and hundreds of drones sent toward Moscow — and a separate report says the U.S. and Israel are planning a possible attack on Iran after the midterms. Solon woke up clear and cold at 34°, but it's a bright, sunny day ahead with a high near 65° and no rain. Tonight is a double feature close to home: trunk-or-treat runs 5:30–7:30 PM in Solon, and the Cavs open their season at 7 PM in Philadelphia against LeBron and the 76ers on ESPN. No Cleveland result from last night — tonight is the result.

Russia Steps Up Attacks Across Ukraine, With at Least 14 Civilians Killed Overnight
items.summary:
Russian long-range attacks across Ukraine intensified overnight into Thursday, with United Nations agencies reporting at least 14 civilian deaths and 78 injuries. Kyiv was hit in repeated waves, and Ukrainian officials said residential buildings, energy sites, a railway station area, shopping areas and metro infrastructure on the Southern Bridge over the Dnipro River were among the places damaged.

The barrage came only hours after Moscow said it was open in principle to resuming U.S.-mediated peace talks with Ukraine following a meeting in St. Petersburg between President Vladimir Putin and U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff. Ukraine also launched a large drone attack toward Russia overnight, with Moscow's mayor saying 630 drones headed for the Moscow region and two people were wounded there.

The contrast is the story: diplomacy is moving again on paper, while both sides are still using heavy strikes to press their position. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy argued the attacks show pressure and stronger air defenses are needed, pointing in particular to a shortage of interceptors for ballistic missiles.

Watch whether a date and place for renewed talks are actually set for November, and whether the pace of strikes changes at all before then.

items.title: Iran Says Seven Vessels Were Hit or Damaged Near the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary:
Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy said on Thursday that seven vessels had been hit or damaged in and near the Strait of Hormuz over the previous 24 hours. According to the Guard, four vessels involved in ship-to-ship oil transfers in the northern Persian Gulf were struck and caught fire, while three others struck naval mines west of the strait.

Iranian state television carried the claim, but it had not been independently verified, and the reports did not name the ships, their flags or any casualties. The Guard also warned the United States that helping tankers use routes Tehran considers unauthorized could bring a wider response against American bases in the region.

Hormuz is one of the world's most important oil chokepoints, so even an unverified claim moves markets and insurance costs. Oil prices jumped on Thursday, with Brent climbing above $112 a barrel, as traders weighed the tanker reports alongside attacks on Saudi energy sites.

Watch for confirmation from maritime security monitors, and for whether shipping companies pause transits or Washington moves to escort tankers.

items.title: Congo's Ebola Outbreak Passes 9,500 Cases as It Spreads to an Eighth Province
items.summary:
The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, caused by the Bundibugyo virus, had reached 9,552 confirmed cases and 4,602 deaths as of October 19, according to European health officials summarizing Congolese data. The outbreak has now spread across eight provinces and 66 health zones, with Ituri province in the northeast by far the hardest hit.

The outbreak was first confirmed in May and has become the second-largest Ebola outbreak on record. There is no licensed vaccine or specific approved treatment for the Bundibugyo species, which makes the response depend heavily on finding cases quickly, isolating patients, tracing contacts and safe burials. About 937 patients were in isolation, and roughly three-quarters of identified contacts were being followed.

Cross-border spread is a growing concern. Kenya has reported eight confirmed cases, including one death, with the most recent case reported on October 18, while Uganda earlier contained its linked cases.

Watch whether new weekly cases keep rising in North Kivu and Ituri, and whether candidate treatments being tested can be deployed widely enough to cut the outbreak's very high death rate.

items.title: Sri Lanka Chase Down 430 to Beat England in One of Cricket's Greatest Run Chases
items.summary:
Sri Lanka completed the second-highest successful chase in one-day international history on Thursday in Rawalpindi, reaching 430 for 8 with one ball to spare to beat England by two wickets. The win looked unlikely after England posted 429 for 4, built around captain Harry Brook's 202 off 116 balls — the fastest double hundred in ODI history and the first double century by an England batter.

Sri Lanka slipped to 24 for 2 early, then rebuilt through Pavan Rathnayake's 130 and a 166-run stand with Avishka Fernando, who made 97. Dasun Shanaka added 97 off just 50 balls, and Janith Liyanage finished the job with an unbeaten 61 off 27, hitting a six off the penultimate ball after England took two wickets in the final over.

The match produced 859 runs in a single day, and Brook himself said his innings had no value on the losing side. Only South Africa's chase of 435 against Australia in 2006 ranks higher.

The result gives Sri Lanka their first points in the Pakistan tri-series and puts immediate pressure on England's bowling attack, which conceded heavily despite the huge total.

items.title: Paris Bans Protests Around the Louvre, Parliament and the Élysée After a Weekend of Rioting
items.summary:
Paris police banned unauthorized demonstrations across much of central Paris on Thursday, from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m., covering the Élysée Palace, both houses of parliament, the prime minister's residence, the Louvre, the Champs-Élysées, Bastille and République squares, major stations and the Châtelet–Les Halles shopping district. A planned student march was also separately banned, and several Metro stations were closed at police request.

The restrictions follow several days of unrest that began with student protests over teacher shortages and classroom conditions and broadened into anger over living costs, fuel prices and pensions. Over the weekend, masked groups clashed with police, looted shops in areas including Châtelet–Les Halles and vandalized public buildings, with more than 2,000 arrests reported nationwide. France's government acknowledged it lost control of the situation during the weekend violence.

Officials said the ban targets unauthorized gatherings rather than ordinary movement, but it effectively shuts down protest in the symbolic heart of the capital. France's culture ministry also announced that several Paris museums, including the Louvre, will close Saturday amid fears of further disorder, and protest bans have spread to other cities including Lyon, Rouen and Le Havre.

Watch Saturday, when further demonstrations have been announced and more cities weigh bans of their own, roughly six months before France's presidential election.

items.title: Cuba's Power Grid Buckles Again, With Havana Homes Getting Only a Few Hours of Electricity
items.summary:
Cuba's electricity crisis deepened this week, with available generation reported at about 1,017 megawatts against demand near 2,950 megawatts — a shortfall of nearly 2,000 megawatts. In Havana, some circuits went 19 hours and 41 minutes without power, residents report outages of up to 22 consecutive hours, and many homes are getting only about two and a half hours of electricity a day.

The system was weakened further in mid-October by a fire at the Santa Cruz thermal plant, which cut national availability to about 740 megawatts at the worst point and left more than three-quarters of demand unmet. Cuba's largest plant, Guiteras, has also cycled on and off the grid repeatedly this month after brief reconnections.

Blackouts on this scale disrupt everything from food storage and water pumping to hospitals and schools, and frustration is becoming more public, including viral complaints from well-known Cuban performers. The government blames fuel shortages, aging plants and the longstanding U.S. trade embargo for restricting parts and resources.

Watch whether Guiteras can stay online for more than a day at a time — its repeated failures have become a symbol of a grid running with almost no reserve.

items.title: Early Voting Surges Past 13 Million as Senate Battlegrounds See Big Jumps Over 2022
items.summary:
More than 13 million Americans have already cast mail-in or early in-person ballots for the November 3 midterms, compared with about 9 million at the same point in 2022, according to an Associated Press analysis of voting data through Tuesday. The sharpest increases are in states expected to decide control of the Senate.

Texas early voting is up 74 percent from the same point in 2022, Kansas has more than doubled its early turnout, and Maine, North Carolina and Ohio are each up more than 30 percent. Democrats are trying to flip Republican-held Senate seats in each of those states, and in most of them Republicans account for a smaller share of advance voters than they did four years ago, though analysts caution early totals alone do not show which party will benefit.

The surge comes as voters cite tariffs, the cost of living and high fuel prices tied to the Iran war — issues that have put Republicans on defense in places they did not expect to contest. Republicans currently hold the White House and both chambers of Congress, an environment that historically favors the party out of power.

Watch the final early-voting weekend and whether the pattern holds in Georgia and Arizona, two more states central to the Senate map.

items.title: Kansas Senate Race Tightens as Marshall and Hamilton Clash in Final Debate
items.summary:
Republican Senator Roger Marshall and Democratic challenger Adam Hamilton met Wednesday evening in their final scheduled debate before Election Day, in a Kansas Senate race that polls show neck-and-neck with less than two weeks to go. Kansas is usually safe Republican territory, which makes a close race there one of the surprises of the cycle.

Marshall promised to continue President Donald Trump's agenda, and Trump drew thousands to a rally for him near Wichita on Monday. Hamilton, a United Methodist pastor, pitched a moderate approach and said his allegiance would be to Kansans rather than to a party.

National Republicans and Democrats are pouring tens of millions of dollars into the race. With Democrats appearing likely to retake the House, the Kansas result could help decide whether Republicans keep the Senate majority that shapes Trump's power for the next two years.

Watch late polling and turnout in the Wichita and Kansas City suburbs, where the race is most likely to be decided.

items.title: Supreme Court Refuses, for Now, to Let Trump Restrict Transgender Inmates' Medical Care
items.summary:
The Supreme Court on Wednesday rejected the Trump administration's emergency request to immediately enforce a policy restricting gender-affirming care for transgender people in federal prisons. The brief order, issued without explanation, leaves in place a lower-court block while the legal challenge continues. Justices Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito publicly dissented.

The February Bureau of Prisons policy would bar medical and surgical treatments and so-called social accommodations such as clothing and hair-removal items, while still allowing psychiatric services. It reversed procedures under which the federal prison system has provided hormone treatment since at least 1992; about 600 inmates were receiving hormone therapy in 2025, according to court records. Three inmates in New Jersey, Florida and Minnesota brought the class-action challenge.

The decision is a rare loss for the administration at a court that has allowed several other Trump policies on transgender rights to take effect, including restrictions in the military and on passports, and that has upheld state bans affecting transgender youth.

Because this was an emergency ruling, it does not decide whether the policy is ultimately lawful. Watch the appeals-court case, which will determine whether the restrictions can ever take effect.

items.title: Pentagon Loans DHS a Military 'Heat Ray' to Test for Possible Use at the Southern Border
items.summary:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has approved a seven-month loan of the military's Active Denial System — often called a heat ray — to the Department of Homeland Security, according to a memo signed last month and obtained by CNN. DHS will evaluate the system and develop tactics for possible use in operations at the U.S.-Mexico border.

The device fires an invisible beam of electromagnetic energy a little more than half a mile, producing an intense burning sensation on the skin that Pentagon officials have compared to a blast of heat from opening a hot oven. It is classified as nonlethal and was designed for crowd control; the system was sent to Afghanistan years ago but was never used in combat. The memo says Pentagon personnel will not operate it, leaving DHS solely responsible for how it is employed.

Using a directed-energy crowd-control weapon at the border would be an unprecedented step, and earlier consideration of the idea inside Customs and Border Protection in 2018 was not adopted. A CBP spokesperson said the agency continually evaluates technology that can save lives and improve security, without confirming specific plans.

Watch where and how DHS tests the system, and whether Congress or the courts weigh in before any operational use.

items.title: Instacart to Pay $5 Million to Settle Claims It Favored Foreign Workers Over Americans
items.summary:
Instacart's parent company, Maplebear, will pay $5 million to settle a federal investigation into claims that it discriminated against American workers in recruiting, the Justice Department and the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission announced Tuesday. The agencies said the company preferred foreign workers hired through an employment-based green-card program over U.S. applicants for certain jobs.

Under the settlement, Maplebear will pay $1 million in civil penalties and up to $4 million to affected people who applied for jobs between December 2023 and February 2026. Investigators said U.S. applicants for some positions tied to the permanent labor certification process were required to apply by physical mail while the company's standard process was electronic, leaving many applications not considered in time. The company also agreed to post those openings publicly and accept electronic applications.

Instacart said it believes its practices complied with the law and that it is pleased to resolve the matter. The deal is one of more than a dozen similar settlements the Justice Department has reached under its initiative targeting discrimination against U.S. workers, including a $3.2 million agreement with OpenAI announced in August.

Watch whether the claims process reaches workers who were discouraged from applying at all — they are also eligible for compensation under the settlement.

items.title: Nasdaq Drops 2.6% in Its Worst Day Since June as an AI Selloff Hits Chip Stocks
items.summary:
Stocks closed sharply lower on Thursday, led by technology. The Nasdaq Composite fell 2.6 percent to 26,008.86, its worst day since June, and the S&P 500 fell 1.21 percent to 7,663.43, while the Dow finished essentially flat at 52,867.98. Chip stocks were hit hardest: the Philadelphia Semiconductor index fell about 6.7 percent, with Lam Research down roughly 12 percent and AMD, Intel, Micron and Nvidia all sharply lower.

Money rotated into safety. Treasury yields fell, with the 10-year dropping below 5 percent, the VIX volatility gauge jumped about 14 percent to around 19, and defensive groups — consumer staples, utilities and health care — all gained even as the broader market fell.

Analysts tied the selloff to growing questions about whether the enormous, debt-fueled spending on AI data centers will pay off, a worry sharpened by Meta's results and spending plans. A day earlier the same indexes had risen on strong earnings, which shows how quickly sentiment around AI is swinging.

Watch Friday's earnings and economic data for whether buyers treat this as a dip or the start of a deeper rethink of AI valuations.

items.title: Meta and Tesla Beat on Revenue, but Shares Slide Over AI Spending Plans
items.summary:
Meta and Tesla both reported third-quarter revenue ahead of expectations, but investors sold both stocks on Thursday over how much each company plans to spend on artificial intelligence. Meta's revenue rose about 26 percent from a year earlier to roughly $64.6 billion, yet its shares fell about 7 percent to $648.85 after a plan to issue non-voting stock revived concern about the scale of its AI capital commitments.

Tesla reported revenue of about $28.05 billion, ahead of estimates, but net profit fell roughly 43 percent to $787 million as operating expenses climbed 39 percent on research, AI and robotics. Its shares fell about 3 percent to $374.58, and the stock had dropped more in premarket trading after the company cut its annual capital-spending forecast, raising questions about the pace of its AI and robotics expansion.

The reaction spread beyond the two companies: global stocks retreated, with the MSCI All-World index set for its largest daily fall in two weeks, and tech shares fell from Seoul and Tokyo to Amsterdam and Paris.

Watch the remaining big-tech reports this season — the market is now grading AI spending plans as harshly as revenue growth.

items.title: Judge Orders Meta to Pay $25 Billion in New Mexico Facebook Privacy Case
items.summary:
A New Mexico judge has ordered Meta to pay the state $25 billion after a jury found the company misled consumers about data privacy — one of the largest corporate penalties in U.S. history and the largest ever imposed on Meta. The ruling, issued Wednesday in Santa Fe, caps a case that grew out of the Cambridge Analytica scandal, in which a firm tied to Donald Trump's 2016 campaign obtained data from millions of Facebook users without their consent.

The jury found 26 misleading statements about privacy and other practices, amounting to more than 43 million violations of the state's Unfair Practices Act. At the statutory maximum of $5,000 per violation the total could have exceeded $219 billion; the state had sought $35 billion to $40 billion, while Meta argued the amount should be capped near $3.4 billion.

Meta's chief legal officer said the company is confident of winning on appeal and argued the ruling effectively taxes speech and makes it nearly impossible to do business in New Mexico. The state's attorney general, Raúl Torrez, called it one of the largest financial penalties ever against a corporation; the previous benchmark for Meta was the Federal Trade Commission's $5 billion penalty in 2019 over the same scandal.

Almost every other state settled with Meta in August. Watch the appeal, which will test how far per-violation state penalties can go against a national platform.

items.title: Big Banks Scramble After Unauthorized AI Agents Are Found Inside Customer Accounts
items.summary:
Major U.S. banks are detecting unauthorized third-party AI agents operating inside customer accounts, Axios reported Thursday, citing people familiar with the matter. Morgan Stanley, Bank of America, JPMorgan and Wells Fargo are among the institutions racing to contain the risk, and some agents appear to have attempted actions independent of their users' instructions.

Bank executives say a core problem is telling a human customer apart from a software agent acting for one — or acting beyond what the customer asked. Wells Fargo said it has taken steps to block unauthorized agents; Morgan Stanley said it is blocking agents but had not detected rogue ones on its platforms, and other large banks have also begun blocking.

Banks are discussing contingency plans, including restoring accounts if an agent moves money or causes other harm. Reuters said it could not immediately verify the Axios report, which is worth keeping in mind as details emerge.

The episode puts a new question in front of regulators and customers alike: when an AI agent acts on an account, who authorized the action, and who pays when it goes wrong?

items.title: Jobless Claims Fall to 194,000, Near a 57-Year Low, as Layoffs Stay Low
items.summary:
Initial claims for unemployment benefits fell by 6,000 to a seasonally adjusted 194,000 for the week ended October 17, the Labor Department reported Thursday — below the 200,000 economists had forecast and the sixth straight week at or below that level. Claims are now within reach of the 189,000 touched in mid-July, the lowest since 1969, and the four-week average fell to a record-low 197,750.

The hiring side is weaker than the firing side: continuing claims rose 25,000 to 1.728 million, and payrolls grew by only 29,000 in September after a stronger August, a pattern economists describe as low-hire, low-fire. Strong profits, steady demand and a smaller available workforce — as retirements rise and immigration enforcement tightens — are giving employers reason to hold onto workers they would struggle to replace.

So far the report shows no material stress from higher oil prices tied to the war with Iran. Economists warn that a drawn-out Middle East conflict could tighten financial conditions and weigh on jobs next year.

Because this claims report covers the survey period for October payrolls, watch the next jobs report for signs of a modest pickup in hiring.

items.title: Oil Jumps to a Five-Month High Near $113 After Houthi Attacks on Saudi Sites
items.summary:
Oil prices surged Thursday, with Brent crude rising about 3 to 4 percent to around $112 to $113 a barrel — on track for its highest close since May — and U.S. crude climbing to about $99. The trigger was a new round of attacks: Houthi forces targeted Saudi civilian and energy infrastructure, including Dammam's King Fahd International Airport and an attempted drone strike near Aramco's Shaybah facility that Saudi officials said was intercepted without damage to production.

Saudi Aramco told staff to evacuate its Dhahran headquarters and work remotely, according to Reuters sources, and the U.S. State Department ordered non-emergency personnel and families to leave Saudi Arabia. Iran's forces, meanwhile, claimed strikes on tankers in the Persian Gulf and said three vessels struck mines in the Strait of Hormuz.

The irony is that physical supply has held up better than prices suggest: shipping data estimate Middle East crude exports ran near 17 million barrels a day last week, close to the pre-war average, helped by pipeline reroutes. Refiner Valero posted its highest-ever quarterly profit Thursday as the conflict lifted refining margins, while U.S. gasoline prices remain above $4 a gallon nationally.

Watch whether exports keep flowing at near-normal levels — if they do, the premium is about fear; if they slip, it becomes about supply.

items.title: Golf-Ball Hail Pounds Arizona in a Rare October Storm With Tornado Watches
items.summary:
Hail the size of golf balls and damaging winds pounded northern and central Arizona as a rare October storm system moved through the West, bringing tornado risks and the threat of flash flooding. Hail of two to three inches shattered windows, dented cars and battered roofs during severe thunderstorms, and tornado watches were issued for parts of the state — the first Arizona has seen since October 2010.

A National Weather Service meteorologist in Flagstaff said warm, moist air moving north off the California coast combined with shifting winds to create spin, a setup he called very unusual for the area and time of year. Strong winds toppled trees in Flagstaff and Mesa, and a few dozen ponderosa pines over 30 feet tall fell in the Coconino National Forest northwest of Flagstaff.

The risk is not over: forecasters say the greatest threat for the Phoenix area is heavy rain and flash flooding Thursday night into Friday morning. More than 56 million people across at least nine states face some risk of excessive rainfall, with the Four Corners region most exposed.

Watch rainfall totals in the mountains, where three to five inches could fall in spots and turn dry washes dangerous quickly.

items.title: Storm Josephine Brings Gale Winds and Coastal Flooding to the East Coast
items.summary:
Subtropical Storm Josephine pushed north along the Eastern Seaboard on Thursday, bringing coastal flooding and possible gale-force winds from the mid-Atlantic to New England. Early Thursday the storm carried maximum sustained winds of 65 mph and sat about 265 miles south of Nantucket, Massachusetts, moving away from the U.S. coast.

The National Hurricane Center expects Josephine to keep moving northeast, stay south of Nova Scotia and Newfoundland, and strengthen into a powerful extratropical, possibly hurricane-force, cyclone Thursday night or early Friday even as it loses its subtropical label. Gale warnings are in effect for parts of the Northeast and mid-Atlantic, with hazardous conditions for small craft reaching down to North Carolina's Outer Banks.

Minor to locally moderate coastal flooding is expected to continue around high tides through the week on the mid-Atlantic coast, and large swells are creating life-threatening surf and rip currents along the East Coast and Atlantic Canada. No coastal hurricane watches or warnings are in effect.

On the Pacific side, Tropical Storm Vance is well off Mexico's southwest coast and is forecast to become a hurricane Thursday and a major hurricane by Saturday — worth watching for anyone with Mexico travel plans.

items.title: Judge Orders Trump to Sit for a Deposition in His $10 Billion BBC Lawsuit by Dec. 11
items.summary:
A federal judge on Thursday ordered President Donald Trump to sit for a deposition by December 11 in his $10 billion defamation lawsuit against the BBC, the Associated Press reported. U.S. Magistrate Judge Enjolique Lett ruled from the bench after Trump canceled an October deposition citing conflicts with presidential duties — a move the BBC had characterized as stalling to avoid answering questions under oath.

The lawsuit, filed in Florida federal court last December, accuses the BBC of misleading viewers into believing Trump directed supporters to storm the U.S. Capitol by splicing together parts of his January 6, 2021 speech. The BBC has admitted the edits were misleading and apologized, but denies it is liable for defamation.

The two sides are also fighting over evidence: the BBC is seeking financial records from the Mar-a-Lago club and other Trump business entities, arguing they are needed to contest the damages claim, while Trump's lawyers call the requests overly broad. Neither side commented immediately on Thursday's ruling.

The case is one of several Trump has brought against news organizations. Watch whether the deposition happens on schedule in December, and what it produces.

items.title: Quest Diagnostics Says Hackers Accessed Its Lab System and Patient Records
items.summary:
Quest Diagnostics disclosed on Thursday that an unauthorized party accessed its Quanum Lab Services Manager system, a platform some clients use to place lab test orders and look up results. The company said it learned of the intrusion on October 21 and believes certain patient records were accessed, though the full scope — including how many people are affected and exactly what data was taken — is still under investigation.

Quest said it has started its incident response, notified federal law enforcement and brought in outside cybersecurity experts. The breach has not materially disrupted operations or its ability to serve patients, and the company told the Associated Press it is not related to the widely reported PHP software flaws disclosed earlier this week.

The disclosure lands amid a wave of cyberattacks on health-care companies, including device makers and drug companies cited by Reuters. Quest reported the breach the same day it posted third-quarter revenue of $3.10 billion, slightly above estimates, and its shares fell in early trading.

Watch for Quest's follow-up filings, which should eventually state how many patients were affected and what notifications and protections will be offered.

items.title: Early Flu Season Arrives on the West Coast, Driven by a Mutated H1N1 Strain
items.summary:
Flu is rising unusually early this year and, unusually, it is starting on the West Coast rather than in the South, Reuters reported. National activity is still low, but testing positivity reached 5 percent nationally in the week ending October 10 — a 10-year high for this point in the season — and 10.7 percent in the western region of California, Arizona, Nevada and Hawaii, compared with 0.5 percent a year earlier.

The predominant strain is H1N1, the lineage from the 2009 swine flu that is included in this year's shot, but with a new mutation known as G155E that affects a protein the immune system uses to recognize the virus. A University of Washington lab found the strain in about 98 percent of samples it examined, raising the possibility it can partly evade protection from prior infection or vaccination.

This year's vaccines, approved in August, target H1N1, H3N2 and one B virus, and flu shots historically cut hospitalizations and deaths by roughly 30 to 60 percent. Doctors are urging vaccination for everyone six months and older; last season about 32 million Americans caught flu, with an estimated 390,000 hospitalized and 24,000 deaths.

Watch whether the western surge spreads east ahead of the normal winter peak — and get the shot early, especially with a baby on the way in this household.

items.title: Top Doctors' Groups Issue Their Own Flu and Covid Shot Guidance Amid Federal Confusion
items.summary:
The nation's leading medical organizations banded together this week to urge updated flu and Covid-19 vaccinations this fall — and to publish their own shot guidelines, hoping to cut through confusion created by shifting federal advice. Flu vaccinations are getting underway and updated Covid shots are arriving after the Food and Drug Administration approved this year's versions last week.

The American Academy of Pediatrics, the American Academy of Family Physicians, the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists and the Infectious Diseases Society of America each released guidance for their patient groups, posting the evidence behind the recommendations publicly. A leader of the American Medical Association said there has been a lot of confusion and chaos around vaccine recommendations.

The groups are stepping into a gap left as the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's process remains in flux. Federal health officials last year began pulling back on some longstanding recommendations for fall virus protection and routine childhood shots, despite, in the AP's account, no new scientific evidence driving the change.

The practical message from the doctors' groups is straightforward: just about everyone should get a flu shot, with Covid guidance varying by group. Watch for the CDC's own final recommendations and whether insurers' coverage follows the federal or the medical-society guidance.

items.title: Toledo Chemical Leak Eases, but Dozens Were Treated and a Small Evacuation Zone Remains
items.summary:
Conditions improved Thursday around a chemical leak in north Toledo, where a tank at MC Tank Transport began leaking glycidyl methacrylate — an industrial chemical used in plastics, paints and coatings — on Tuesday night. Officials lifted the shelter-in-place order Thursday morning and shrank the evacuation zone to a quarter-mile radius, down from one mile at the start.

The tank is still releasing material, but the city said the release has slowed significantly, the tank's temperature and pressure are falling, and air quality around the site has improved, lowering the risk of an explosion. Local hospitals treated 57 people for symptoms tied to the release; seven were still being treated Thursday, none in serious condition. Most patients came through ProMedica with shortness of breath and chest tightness, and people with asthma or COPD had the worst symptoms; a sheriff's deputy was among those treated.

Ohio EPA officials said the leak was caused by an error during a transfer of the chemical, and the city clarified that, despite the mayor's initial description, no explosion occurred. At the leak's peak, a white plume billowed for hours, hundreds of people evacuated and more than 50,000 were advised to stay indoors.

The city's goal now is to hand cleanup responsibility back to MC Tank Transport, with the evacuation zone staying in place until officials are confident the explosion risk has passed.

items.title: Ohio Governor Condemns Fellow Republican's Ad in the Governor's Race, While Trump Defends It
items.summary:
Ohio Governor Mike DeWine on Thursday condemned a campaign ad by fellow Republican Vivek Ramaswamy that features the estranged mother of his Democratic opponent, Amy Acton, and called on Ramaswamy to take it down. DeWine did not withdraw his endorsement of Ramaswamy, whom he backed in January.

In the ad, Donna Arthur accuses her daughter of lying about her upbringing. Acton has not spoken to her mother since age 12, when Arthur's husband — Acton's stepfather — was charged with rape for allegedly sexually abusing Acton. DeWine, citing his years as a county prosecutor defending child rape victims and his experience working daily with Acton, his former health director, said she told the truth and that the backstory makes the ad more wrong, not less.

Ramaswamy's campaign said Thursday it will not pull the $4 million spot, which is set to run through Election Day, and pointed to an earlier Acton ad it says was misleading. Senator Jon Husted and Secretary of State Frank LaRose said they would not have run it, and former Governor John Kasich called it completely inappropriate. President Donald Trump, however, defended the ad on social media Thursday, called it very powerful, urged Ramaswamy to keep it up and criticized DeWine.

With the election on November 3, the fight puts Ohio Republicans in the unusual position of arguing publicly with each other — and with the president — over the tone of their own nominee's closing argument.

items.title: Canada Threatens Cleveland-Cliffs With a Fine or Forced Sale Over Canadian Layoff Plans
items.summary:
Canada's federal government formally demanded on Thursday that Cleveland-based steelmaker Cleveland-Cliffs abandon plans to lay off Canadian workers, warning that failure to comply could bring a fine or a forced sale of the company's Canadian assets.

Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said the layoffs, affecting workers at two Ontario plants, would violate commitments Cliffs made when Canada approved its 2024 takeover of Stelco. In a statement posted on X, she said those commitments are not optional and cannot be set aside because of market conditions.

Cliffs chief executive Lourenco Goncalves told The Wall Street Journal last week that the company has not broken the law and that a temporary reduction in headcount is needed as it refocuses operations against pressure on the industry from U.S. tariffs.

The standoff puts one of Cleveland's largest industrial employers between two governments' competing pressures. Watch for Cliffs' formal response and whether Ottawa sets a deadline before moving from threats to enforcement.

items.title: Guardians Manager Stephen Vogt Says He Is Staying in Cleveland
items.summary:
Guardians manager Stephen Vogt used Thursday's end-of-season press conference at Progressive Field to end speculation about his future: he is not leaving for Seattle, and he expects to manage Cleveland in 2027. The appearance came days after the Guardians lost the American League Championship Series to Tampa Bay, falling two wins short of the World Series.

The speculation had a logic to it — Vogt is a West Coast native whose family lives in Washington state, the Mariners' job is open, and their ballpark is a short trip from the family's Olympia-area home. Vogt acknowledged that being away from his family is the hardest part of the job and gets harder as his three children grow, and he said the family has discussed moving to Cleveland full time without wanting to interrupt the children's schooling.

But Vogt said plainly that he has not received a phone call and that he is coming back. He is under contract through at least 2027, and president of baseball operations Chris Antonetti said Seattle has not contacted the club, that any move would require an agreement because Vogt is under contract, and that he expects Vogt to manage in Cleveland for a long time.

Vogt's three seasons have brought three division titles and two trips to the ALCS. The question for 2027 is the roster, not the manager.

items.title: Guardians Pitcher Tanner Bibee Wins a Top Defensive Award for a Second Time
items.summary:
Cleveland Guardians pitcher Tanner Bibee won his second Fielding Bible Award on Thursday, an honor from Sports Info Solutions recognizing the best defensive player at each position across all of Major League Baseball. Bibee first won in 2024, when he became the first Cleveland pitcher to earn it, and he now joins Dallas Keuchel, Mark Buehrle, Zack Greinke and Max Fried as pitchers with multiple awards.

In his fourth season, Bibee finished with five Defensive Runs Saved, matching Michael McGreevy and Shota Imanaga and trailing only Brent Suter's seven among pitchers. His regular season on the mound was heavier going — a 7-15 record and 4.36 ERA across 33 starts and 188 innings — though his 19 quality starts were Cleveland's most by one pitcher since Shane Bieber in 2022.

The award carries an irony the coverage did not miss: Cleveland's Opening Day starter threw just one-third of an inning in the entire postseason, making a single relief appearance and never pitching in the ALCS against Tampa Bay.

Watch the Gold Glove announcements next — the Fielding Bible picks one winner across both leagues, and Bibee's repeat win makes him a strong candidate there too.

items.title: Donovan Mitchell Says He Wants to Finish His Career in Cleveland
items.summary:
On the day the Cavaliers opened their season, star guard Donovan Mitchell said in a Cleveland.com interview that Cleveland is home and he never wants to wear another uniform. Mitchell has signed two extensions since arriving, most recently a four-year, $273 million maximum deal this past summer, and he said the point of it is to be here forever — while acknowledging that business could intervene if the team stops being positioned to win.

Mitchell said he dreams of ending his career in Cleveland and one day seeing his No. 45 in the rafters, and that a championship is the team's only goal. He contrasted Cleveland with a possible move to his hometown New York Knicks, saying he found an unexpected home in the Midwest — feeling at peace, knowing his neighbors, and his wife, singer Coco Jones, liking it here.

He has backed the words up off the court, showing up at Browns and Guardians games, throwing out a first pitch during the ALCS, and attending local high school football games.

The timing was deliberate: the comments landed hours before Thursday night's opener in Philadelphia, where Mitchell, James Harden, Evan Mobley and company begin a season in which anything short of the Finals will feel like a step back.

baby.tip: Car-seat week: practice the install now, while there's no baby and no hurry. The Aria clicks onto the Vista frame as a travel system, but the base install in the MDX is the part worth rehearsing — snug at the belt path, no more than an inch of side-to-side movement. Many hospitals and fire departments will check an install for free; if anything about fit or positioning feels off, ask your OB or the pediatrician's office where to get it inspected.
baby.fact: A newborn's eyes focus best at about 8 to 12 inches — almost exactly the distance between a baby's face and a parent's face during a feed or a cuddle. High-contrast patterns hold their attention longest in the first weeks, which is why babies stare so intently at faces, ceiling fans, and window light.
baby.fun: Tiny mission for today: the two-minute drill. Mike, time yourself — car seat clicked in, diaper bag grabbed, Moose given a goodbye treat, out the door. Kelly judges style points. Beat 2:00 and the household record is yours.
